baa_10y_spread.proxy_note: Moody's Baa corporate bond yield minus the 10Y Treasury -- a long-run investment-grade credit-risk-premium PROXY, not the literal ICE BofA IG OAS series this system quotes daily. Real history back to 1986. Useful for direction and episode timing (did credit broadly tighten/widen, and when); its magnitude runs tighter than IG OAS and far tighter than HY OAS, so never quote its level as if it were either.

history_digest.sentence: The 10-year Treasury yield (5.24%) first reached this level on Sep 28 and has been there on 9 of the 10 sessions since; before this run, the last time was Jun 2007, and only briefly (3 sessions between Jun 2006 and Jun 2007); it was last there routinely until May 2002. This run's high was 5.31% on Oct 5, last matched in May 2002. Today's reading is at or above the reading on 87 of every 100 days of the last 30 years, but about average (49th percentile) since 1962. Every reading in the 1970s and 1980s was at or above today's 5.24%.

history_digest.sentence: The 10-year TIPS real yield (2.87%) has been at or above this level since Sep 28; before this run, the last time was Nov 2008 (during the 2007-09 Global Financial Crisis). This run's high was 2.95% on Oct 5, last matched in Nov 2008. Today's reading is at or above the reading on 99.6 of every 100 days since 2003. But TIPS only exist since 2003: the Cleveland Fed's model real rate, back to 1982, puts real rates at the 80th percentile of the last 30 years and the 54th since 1982 — high against the last 30 years, about average since 1982.

history_digest.sentence: The 10-year Treasury yield is up 106bp this year — the 8th-largest rise through this date in 64 years (bigger: 1987 +271bp, 2022 +237bp, 1981 +230bp, …). Over the last 12 months it is up 1.10 points; a 12-month rise at least that big has started 14 times since 1963 (not counting 2 that lasted under 10 sessions). Measured from each start, the S&P 500 (price only) was lower a year later in 5 of 14 (any 12-month stretch since 1962: 24.4%), and a recession began within two years in 6 of 13, covering 5 different recessions (any two-year stretch since 1962 outside a recession: 27.4%; 1 more began mid-recession).
